scenes.text: Count the spirals on a sunflower, and you'll often find a famous math sequence.
It goes one, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, and on forever.
Each number is simply the two before it added together.
That's why November twenty third is Fibonacci Day: eleven, twenty three.
One sunflower head had fifty five spirals going one way and thirty four the other.
Both are neighbors in the sequence.
Pinecones and pineapples often show eight and thirteen.
The trick: each new seed grows at about one hundred thirty seven and a half degrees from the last.
This golden angle puts every seed in the least crowded spot.
Divide any number in the sequence by the one before, and you get closer and closer to one point six one eight.
The sequence is named after Leonardo of Pisa, who lived around the year twelve hundred.
He shared it in his book Liber Abaci, using a puzzle about breeding rabbits.
But Indian scholars knew these numbers long before him.
And nature isn't perfect: a study of six hundred fifty seven sunflowers found some were frankly weird.
Have you ever counted the spirals on a pinecone?

title: Sunflowers secretly count in Fibonacci 🌻
caption: Nov 23 is Fibonacci Day (11/23). Sunflower heads often have spiral counts like 34 and 55, neighbors in the Fibonacci sequence, because each seed sits about 137.5° from the last. Not every flower follows the rule!
